# Preface {.unnumbered}

This book is a guide to **ISLA** (Invariant Slice Attention), a neural
surrogate for steady, boundary-driven PDE problems: given the surface of a
body and the conditions it sits in, ISLA predicts the steady field on that
surface and in the domain around it, in a fraction of a second where a
solver takes hours. It is written for a reader fluent in PDEs, numerics and
optimization who has not met this model, and perhaps not the transformer
machinery behind it. Every term is defined where it first appears, and
every number is computed from a checked-in result file as the page renders.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Where the name comes from"}
An *isla* is an island: a shape defined entirely by its boundary. The
boundary is what the method takes as input. The code is
`physicsnemo.experimental.models.ISLA`.
:::

```{python}
#| label: setup-index
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
import standing as S
from matplotlib.colors import TwoSlopeNorm

ROWS = S.headline_rows()
def verdicts():
    out = {"leads": [], "is level with": [], "trails": [], "is not compared with": []}
    for k, f, lab in ROWS:
        s = S.Standing(k)
        for a in S.BASELINES:
            if s.has(a):
                out[s.verdict(a, f)].append((k, f, a))
    return out
V = verdicts()
n_pairs = sum(len(v) for k, v in V.items() if k != "is not compared with")
UNFAIR = [S.DATASETS[k].short for k in S.available() if not S.DATASETS[k].fair_drive]
SURF = [k for k in S.available() if "area" in S.DATASETS[k].protocols]
FLOW = [k for k in S.available() if k not in ("tensile2d", "lug", "deepjeb")]
SOLID = [k for k in S.available() if k in ("tensile2d", "lug", "deepjeb")]
def shifts(ks, archs, protocol):
    """Every headline field's error under a protocol over its native error, for the given datasets and architectures."""
    return [S.Standing(k).shift(a, f, protocol) for k in ks for f in S.DATASETS[k].headline for a in archs]
isla_area = max(abs(x - 1) for x in shifts(SURF, ["ISLA"], "area"))
base_area = min(shifts(SURF, S.BASELINES, "area"))
isla_posed = max(abs(x - 1) for x in shifts(FLOW, ["ISLA"], "posed"))
base_posed_flow = (min(shifts(FLOW, S.BASELINES, "posed")), max(shifts(FLOW, S.BASELINES, "posed")))
base_posed_solid = (min(shifts(SOLID, S.BASELINES, "posed")), max(shifts(SOLID, S.BASELINES, "posed")))
tie_shift = {k: max(shifts([k], ["ISLA"], "posed")) for k in ("tensile2d", "lug")}
```

## The thesis {#sec-verdict}

```{python}
#| label: para-thesis
#| output: asis
print(
    "**ISLA is a slice-attention transformer that is exactly equivariant to rigid motions and consistent under a change of "
    "mesh, by construction, and in distribution it is about as accurate as the strongest models of its family.** It is measured "
    "against Transolver and its geometry-aware successor GeoTransolver, two published slice-attention surrogates, each at its own "
    "reference configuration and scored the same way. "
    f"Over the {n_pairs} comparisons of @fig-standing (each headline field of each dataset against each baseline"
    + (f"; {' and '.join(UNFAIR)} are not counted, because in their records the baselines read the freestream as a raw "
       "physical vector" if UNFAIR else "")
    + f"), ISLA leads in {len(V['leads'])}, is level in {len(V['is level with'])} and trails in {len(V['trails'])}. "
    f"Rotate and translate the test geometry, and on the {len(FLOW)} flow tasks every baseline error grows "
    f"{base_posed_flow[0]:.0f}-fold to {base_posed_flow[1]:.0f}-fold while ISLA's stays within {100 * isla_posed:.1f}% of its native value. "
    f"On the {len(SOLID)} solid-mechanics tasks the baselines' grow {base_posed_solid[0]:.1f}-fold to {base_posed_solid[1]:.0f}-fold; "
    f"ISLA's is unchanged on DeepJEB++ and moves up to {tie_shift['tensile2d']:.2f}-fold on Tensile2d and {tie_shift['lug']:.1f}-fold "
    "on the lug, where boundary samples tie for nearest and break the symmetry of its interior geometry (@sec-invariances). "
    "Redraw the surface as a uniform point cloud, and every baseline error grows at least "
    f"{base_area:.1f}-fold while ISLA's stays within {100 * isla_area:.1f}%. "
    "Where ISLA trails, and where its own error moves, the book shows the mechanism."
)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-hero
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The problem, on one DrivAerML car. Top: the input is the surface
#|   (here 150,000 of its 17 million cells) and the far-field direction;
#|   the output on a surface task is the field on it, here the pressure
#|   coefficient $C_p = (p - p_\infty)/\tfrac12\rho U_\infty^2$ from the
#|   reference solution. Bottom: on an interior task the output is the
#|   flow around the body, here the velocity magnitude on the symmetry
#|   plane. How to read this: these are the reference CFD fields, not a
#|   prediction; ISLA's predictions of fields like these, and their errors,
#|   are drawn in the dataset chapters. Data:
#|   results/problem_figures_2026-09-22/drivaer.npz.
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| code-fold: true
D, Dm = load_problem("drivaer")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 5.0), sharex=True, gridspec_kw=dict(hspace=0.12, height_ratios=[1.0, 1.15]))
ax = axes[0]
sp = D["surf_points"]
sc = depth_scatter(ax, sp[:, [0, 2]], sp[:, 1], D["surf_cp"], s=1.6, cmap=DIVERGING, norm=TwoSlopeNorm(vcenter=0.0, vmin=-1.5, vmax=1.0))
map_axes(ax); ax.set_ylabel("z [m]")
cb = fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, fraction=0.03, pad=0.01, extend="min"); cb.outline.set_visible(False); cb.set_label("$C_p$ [–]")
bb = D["surf_bbox"]; ax.annotate("", xy=(bb[0, 0] - 0.2, 0.8), xytext=(bb[0, 0] - 1.1, 0.8), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=INK, lw=2))
ax.text(bb[0, 0] - 0.65, 0.95, r"$\hat g_1$", ha="center", fontsize=11, color=INK)
ax.set_xlim(bb[0, 0] - 1.3, bb[1, 0] + 0.6)
ax = axes[1]
pp = D["slice_points"]; keep = (pp[:, 0] > bb[0, 0] - 1.3) & (pp[:, 0] < bb[1, 0] + 0.6) & (pp[:, 2] < bb[1, 2] + 0.9)
sc = ax.scatter(pp[keep, 0], pp[keep, 2], c=D["slice_umag"][keep], s=1.4, lw=0, cmap=SEQUENTIAL, vmin=0, vmax=1.3, rasterized=True)
map_axes(ax); ax.set_xlabel("x [m]"); ax.set_ylabel("z [m]")
cb = fig.colorbar(sc, ax=ax, fraction=0.03, pad=0.01); cb.outline.set_visible(False); cb.set_label(r"$|u| / U_\infty$ [–]")
plt.show()
```

## The standing in one figure {#sec-standing-index}

```{python}
#| label: fig-standing
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The standing of ISLA against both baselines at their reference
#|   configurations, every dataset and headline field. Left: the native
#|   mesh, as baseline ÷ ISLA, so a mark right of the line favors ISLA;
#|   GeoTransolver (red circles) and Transolver (amber triangles) at the
#|   seed-mean ratio, the faint bar spanning every pairing of a baseline seed
#|   with an ISLA seed; the gray band is the ±3% band inside which two
#|   architectures are called level. Right: what happens to each
#|   architecture's own error when every test case is rotated and translated,
#|   as its error over its native error; ISLA (blue squares) sits at one
#|   except on the lug and Tensile2d, whose boundary samples tie. How to read this: rows are different datasets, fields
#|   and units of difficulty and are not comparable with one another; a row
#|   marked † holds ISLA checkpoints without the normalized slice reads of
#|   its reference configuration; a row marked ‡ has its baselines drawn
#|   hollow and is not compared, because in that record they read the
#|   freestream as a raw physical vector rather than a unit direction
#|   (@sec-hilift, @sec-airfrans). Data: results/char/; every number is in
#|   @tbl-thesis.
#| fig-height: 6.6
#| code-fold: true
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 6.4), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1.35, 1.0], wspace=0.06))
ax = axes[0]
S.plot_native(ax)
ax.set_xlim(0.45, 9.0); ax.set_xticks([0.5, 1, 2, 5]); ax.set_xticklabels(["0.5", "1", "2", "5"])
ax.set_xlabel("native mesh: baseline error ÷ ISLA error [–]")
ax.text(1.05, len(ROWS) - 0.15, "favors ISLA →", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2, va="bottom")
ax.text(0.95, len(ROWS) - 0.15, "← favors the baseline", fontsize=8.5, color=INK2, va="bottom", ha="right")
ax = axes[1]
# one row per dataset and headline field, aligned with the rows on the left
for j, (k, f, lab) in enumerate(ROWS):
    s = S.Standing(k); yy = len(ROWS) - 1 - j
    for arch, key, dy in (("ISLA", "isla_ref", 0.0), ("GeoTransolver", "gt", 0.16), ("Transolver", "t", -0.16)):
        if s.has(arch):
            st = STYLE[key]
            ax.plot(s.shift(arch, f, "posed"), yy + dy, marker=st["marker"], color=st["color"], ms=6.5, mec="white", mew=0.6, ls="none")
ax.axvline(1.0, color=INK2, lw=1.0); ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_ylim(axes[0].get_ylim())
ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.set_xlim(0.8, 900); ax.set_xticks([1, 10, 100]); ax.set_xticklabels(["1", "10", "100"])
ax.set_xlabel("rotated and translated ÷ native, own error [–]")
label_line(ax, 1.15, len(ROWS) - 0.6, "ISLA", BLUE, fontsize=8.5)
label_line(ax, 80, len(ROWS) - 0.6, "GeoTransolver", RED, fontsize=8.5, ha="center")
label_line(ax, 80, len(ROWS) - 1.4, "Transolver", AMBER, fontsize=8.5, ha="center")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| label: para-standing-reading
#| output: asis
def names(items):
    seen = []
    for k, f, a in items:
        t = f"{S.DATASETS[k].name} {S.Standing(k).fields[f]} against {a}"
        seen.append(t)
    return "; ".join(seen)
by = {}
for k, f, a in V["trails"]:
    by.setdefault(k, []).append(f"{S.Standing(k).fields[f]} against {a}")
print(f"**Where ISLA trails** ({len(V['trails'])} of {n_pairs}): "
      + "; ".join(f"on {S.DATASETS[k].name}, {', '.join(v)}" for k, v in by.items())
      + ". Each dataset chapter shows where on the body or in the field the difference sits; the full table, with every seed, "
        "is @tbl-thesis.")
```

## Names and colors {#sec-key-index}

The book names three architectures, always at their reference
configurations unless a caption says otherwise, and gives each a color and
a marker it keeps in every figure.

| | color and mark | reference configuration |
|---|---|---|
| **ISLA** | blue, filled square | width 512, 12 layers, 512 slices, learning rate 3.75e-4, 200,000 training cells |
| **ISLA-DTT** | light blue, open square | ISLA's reference configuration with read-only prediction points (interior tasks) |
| **GeoTransolver** | red, filled circle | width 256 (local width 32), learning rate 1e-3, 200,000 training cells |
| **Transolver** | amber, filled triangle | width 512, 16 layers, learning rate 1e-3, 100,000 training cells |

: The architectures of this book. How to read this: a ratio is always
*baseline ÷ ISLA*, so above one favors ISLA; errors are the area-weighted
relative L2 of @sec-metrics, scored in float32 and averaged over two seeds.
Every name, symbol and color is in @sec-principled-decisions.
{#tbl-key-index}

## How to read this book {#sec-how-to-read}

**The book reads in order, and each chapter assumes only the ones before
it.** Three readers will want different paths through it.

- **To understand the method**, read Parts I and II: the problem and how a
  surrogate is scored (@sec-problem); a field guide to neural PDE
  surrogates, from attention as an integral operator to slice attention
  (@sec-landscape); ISLA one idea at a time (@sec-isla); the two
  invariances it is built for, as contracts and as measurements
  (@sec-invariances); and the forward pass stage by stage, with the code
  and what it costs on a GPU (@sec-architecture).
- **To use it**, read Part III: the configuration, inputs, commands and
  checkpoints (@sec-using) and the benchmark rules every number obeys
  (@sec-baselines). Then the dataset chapter closest to your problem.
- **To judge it**, start with the standing (@sec-standing), then the
  dataset chapters of Part IV, which all follow one order: the problem and
  what varies, what is measured, the standing with pictures of the
  predictions, the studies that belong to that dataset, and what the
  dataset does not say. Then capacity and scaling (@sec-capacity), the
  limits and open questions (@sec-limits), and, for the dated record of
  every experiment, the program status (@sec-program-status) and the lab
  notebook (@sec-notebook).

Optional depth sits in collapsed notes like the one at the top of this
page; the text reads completely with all of them closed.
